name: Plan-Making Effect
summary: Making a specific plan for an unfinished goal stops it from intruding on your thoughts, even though the goal itself is not yet reached.
explanation:
The plan-making effect is the finding that an unfinished goal stops nagging you once you make a concrete plan for it. E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister described it in 2011 in a paper titled "Consider it done!".

Earlier research on the Zeigarnik effect showed that unfinished tasks stay active in memory and intrude on unrelated work. Masicampo and Baumeister reproduced that: participants with an unfulfilled goal had more intrusive thoughts and did worse on an unrelated task. But when the participants made a specific plan (what they would do, when and where), the intrusions and the drop in performance disappeared. The goal was still not done. The plan was enough to tell the mind that it could stop monitoring it.

This explains why capture-and-clarify systems work. In Getting Things Done, writing down an open loop and deciding its next action lets you stop thinking about it. The effect only holds when the plan is specific and you trust that you will follow it. A vague "I will deal with it later" does not close the loop. It is also the mechanism behind the ready-to-resume plan, a short note written before an interruption that reduces attention residue.

Note that the original studies were small lab experiments with students. The direction of the effect fits a large body of goal research, but the exact size in daily life is uncertain.

articles.title: Consider It Done! Plan Making Can Eliminate the Cognitive Effects of Unfulfilled Goals
